A user says their company has run the self-hosted GrowthBook for a few months and is very happy with it, and that issues get resolved quickly. They like that it works on top of existing customer data. They just exposed views over their click-stream data instead of sending data to third parties.

Ping Labs has used GrowthBook for a few weeks. The user was shocked at how much setup a simple feature flag took with services like LaunchDarkly. They had GrowthBook working in roughly 15 minutes with under 10 lines of code changed: "This is all we will need for a long, long time."

BoldVoice has used GrowthBook for ~6 weeks. They found it while considering far more expensive options like Optimizely ("6 figures"). The user says the tooling is pretty intuitive and support has been stellar, but "there's still a ton to build here."
A user had previously struggled to build an internal A/B testing tool. At Miggos they implemented GrowthBook and got feature flags and A/B tests into their Vue frontend in a few hours.

Downside raised: GrowthBook provides feature flags and A/B testing, but you have to bring your own analytics. The user notes a GitHub issue about Matomo integration had been open since September with no docs guide or SQL examples.

Comparison: Optimizely is a walled garden where you must push all metrics as events to it. GrowthBook (like Eppo) connects to your existing data warehouse and supports any metric you can express as a query. Unlike Eppo, GrowthBook is open source with an optional cloud SaaS.

A user asked whether GrowthBook will support gradual "Feature Rollouts" with metric monitoring like Statsig's feature gates and pulse metrics. Their point: with plain flags you build your own logging and analysis, while full experiments are overly constrained by statistical rigor.
A user wanted a way to self-host GrowthBook without the packaged Docker version, so it could run on shared hosting (uberspace) that doesn't support Docker.

Critique of GrowthBook's recommendation to run many experiments in parallel. The user argues this splits a potentially limited sample and risks interaction effects, even when tests are on different pages.
A former Sixpack user says SeatGeek upgraded Sixpack internally to "Sevenpack", but "something like GrowthBook looks much nicer!"

Complaint about the MongoDB dependency: one user said it would be a decently large operational addition to their stack and that a SQL server should suffice. Another said they would likely evaluate and use the product only if it didn't depend on MongoDB, citing its non-open-source SSPL license and reputation.
A user noted the configuration apparently can't be stored in the code repository, which they consider key for treating config as code with versioning and blame. "Otherwise, this looks great."

An A/B experimenter questioned email alerts sent when "significance" is reached. Without minimum sample sizes calculated in advance, they worry this produces Type I errors and leads lay users to believe short tests are statistically sound.
A maintainer of open-source A/B tools (Alephbet), built out of frustration with Optimizely, called GrowthBook "very polished." They noted statistical analysis was always the hardest part for them.
Criticism: "Coupling metrics to experimentation is a huge red flag. You should offload that onto DBT or some other data modeling tools."

A user found little detail on how GrowthBook handles multi-armed bandit and early-stopping problems beyond Bayesian stats with unknown priors. They also worry that drilling down by categories makes significance even more of a concern.
